name: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12
route: Applied to the skin in serums and creams
status: Cosmetic ingredient; not an FDA-approved drug
mechanism: Copies a repeating piece of elastin that, in cell studies, stimulates skin fibroblasts; benefit for wrinkles in people is unproven

article.summary: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is a skincare peptide modeled on a fragment of elastin, marketed for firmness and elasticity. Evidence is mainly cell and skin-sample work, with no large human trial found.
article.takeaway: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is a skincare peptide built on VGVAPG, a six-amino-acid sequence that repeats in elastin, the protein that lets skin spring back. In cultured cells, elastin fragments and the VGVAPG sequence itself stimulated skin fibroblasts to grow,[^1] but VGVAPG also raised production of collagenase (MMP-1), an enzyme that breaks collagen down.[^2] A 2025 study on human skin samples found that the palmitoylated peptide entered the outer layers and strengthened the barrier after lipids were stripped,[^3] which is a mechanical effect rather than proof of wrinkle reduction. **No large human trial** was found.
glance: Serums and creams, usually once or twice daily
Cell and skin-sample studies; no large human trial found

blocks.text: Elastin gives skin its snap. When elastin breaks down, it releases fragments that carry a short motif, VGVAPG. Cells have a receptor that recognizes these fragments, and in lab dishes the signal tells fibroblasts to multiply.[^1] The theory behind this ingredient is that a skin product carrying the motif could trigger a repair response.

The signal is double-edged. The same elastin-peptide receptor pathway turned on MMP-1, a collagen-degrading enzyme, in cultured fibroblasts,[^2] so what a cream would do in living skin is not obvious. Palmitic acid, a fatty acid, is attached to help the peptide mix with skin lipids.

rows: VGVAPG, but not two control sequences, stimulated fibroblast growth at sub-nanomolar concentrations[^1]
VGVAPG raised pro-collagenase-1 (pro-MMP-1) expression through the elastin-binding receptor[^2]
Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 reached the outer layers, formed a gel, and strengthened and repaired the barrier after lipid removal[^3]
Resembled collagen, elastin and fibronectin and lacked the toxin-like features of known harmful peptides[^4]

blocks.text: No randomized trial of wrinkle reduction with this peptide was found. Reviews of anti-aging cosmetics describe good supporting data as often missing.[^5]
It appears in serums, eye creams and moisturizers marketed for firming. Ingredient lists seldom show its concentration, and any effect would take weeks of daily use.

The studies cited here include no human safety trial. Irritation or allergy to the formula is the main practical risk, and the collagenase finding is a reason to want longer, controlled human studies.[^2]
Cosmetics do not need FDA approval before sale, and a product that claims to change how skin works can be treated as a drug.[^6]

Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 rests on elegant biology and early lab data, but its effect on wrinkles in people is unproven and the underlying signal has a possible downside in cell work. It is a reasonable low-risk ingredient to try in a moisturizer, with modest expectations.

evidence.label: Very limited: cell and skin-sample studies
evidence.text: Cell work shows the elastin motif can both stimulate fibroblast growth and increase a collagen-degrading enzyme,[^1][^2] and skin-sample work shows barrier effects.[^3] Controlled wrinkle trials are lacking.[^5]

faq.a: That has not been shown. The cell studies measured fibroblast growth and enzyme expression, not new elastic fibers in living skin.[^1][^2]

faq.q: Is it the same as palmitoyl pentapeptide-4?
faq.a: No. Both are palmitoylated signal peptides, but this one is modeled on elastin and the other on collagen, and each has a different, limited evidence base. See [palmitoyl pentapeptide-4](/peptides/palmitoyl-pentapeptide-4).

faq.q: Can I use it with retinoids or acids?
faq.a: Nothing in the cited studies tests combinations. Peptides are often used alongside other actives, and irritation from the stronger ingredient is the usual concern; a dermatologist can advise on a routine.
